one_liner: WebAssembly blob from the mtcute Telegram library: libdeflate gzip, tgcrypto AES-IGE/CTR and SHA hashes, beating pure-JS equivalents.
what_it_does: @mtcute/wasm is one freestanding C-to-wasm32 module (no Emscripten, no libc) with a thin TypeScript wrapper exposing synchronous Uint8Array functions: deflateMaxSize (zlib-wrapped, level 6, returns null above a size cap), gunzip, ige256Encrypt/ige256Decrypt, createCtr256/ctr256/freeCtr256, sha1 and sha256. You load it once with initSync (bytes, Module or Instance), and getWasmUrl/SIMD_AVAILABLE pick mtcute-simd.wasm when the engine validates SIMD. It is not a drop-in for pako or node:zlib (no streaming, no levels, no gzip compression); mtcute's own Node provider uses it only for AES-IGE, while its web provider uses it for every primitive.
how_it_is_fast: Compiled C replaces JavaScript: a size-trimmed libdeflate (table-driven Huffman decoding, fast matchfinding), tgcrypto's T-table AES-256 (Te0-Te3/Td0-Td3 lookups) with IGE and CTR chaining on 16-byte vector types, teeny-sha1 and LekKit sha256. Per-call overhead is small: the compressor and decompressor are allocated once at init, a bump allocator serves buffers from the heap tail, and key, IV and digest travel through shared static buffers, which is why the biggest wins are on 48-byte payloads (gunzip 9.3x pako, IGE 3.8x @cryptography/aes in ops/s). The gzip path also compiles out CRC32 verification (it relies on MTProto's msg_key integrity) and sizes the output from the gzip ISIZE trailer, removing work the JavaScript and zlib baselines do.
when_to_use: Browser, Deno, Bun or worker Telegram clients that need synchronous AES-IGE/CTR, SHA-1/256 and zlib on MTProto-sized payloads: at 48 B tgcrypto-wasm IGE encrypt ran 1,219,546 vs 322,174 ops/s for @cryptography/aes (3.8x) and libdeflate gunzip 1,095,136 vs 117,917 ops/s for pako (9.3x, derived from page data).

Small authenticated gunzip workloads even on Node: the no-unroll libdeflate build beat zlib.gunzipSync at every size (949,255 vs 162,193 ops/s at 48 B, 4,854 vs 3,301 at 73 KB), partly because it skips the CRC32 check zlib performs.
Bundle-size-sensitive web apps: the committed mtcute.wasm is 57,363 B raw and about 26 KB gzipped for every primitive, against 47.4 KiB rendered / 15.1 KiB gzipped for pako alone (zlib only).
Synchronous hashing where WebCrypto's per-call async overhead dominates: WebCrypto SHA-256 managed 37,005 ops/s at 48 B vs 1,107,333 for lekkit-sha256 wasm.
when_not_to_use: On Node.js for anything except AES-IGE: native OpenSSL does AES-CTR at 1,791 vs 137 MB/s and SHA-256 at 1,065 vs 223 MB/s on 73 KB, and mtcute's own NodeCryptoProvider uses node:crypto and node:zlib for those.
Deflating small payloads with the shipped no-unroll build: it trails Node zlib below 73 KB (29,523 vs 67,343 ops/s at 48 B; 3,521 vs 3,702 at 13 KB), and fast-zlib beats it on small inputs.

As a general gzip decoder or AES library for untrusted or unpadded input: CRC32 is not verified, the output size comes from the gzip trailer, IGE does not check the 16-byte length rule, and the T-table AES is not constant-time.
When SHA-256 speed matters: lekkit-sha256 wasm is about level with pure-JS sha256-uint8array (223 vs 206 MB/s at 73 KB; 50.4 vs 53.4 MB/s at 48 B, slower).
If LGPL-3.0 code is unacceptable: the AES sources under packages/wasm/lib/crypto derive from tgcrypto (LGPL-3.0) inside an otherwise MIT package.

integration.form: module (npm @mtcute/wasm 0.32.0, published 2026-08-27: TypeScript wrapper plus mtcute.wasm and mtcute-simd.wasm)
integration.dependencies: none at runtime (freestanding C, no libc or Emscripten runtime); rebuilding the blobs needs clang 16, lld and binaryen (Dockerfile on alpine:3.18.4)
integration.min_toolchain: any WebAssembly engine with bulk-memory (built with -mbulk-memory); the SIMD blob needs wasm SIMD128; benchmarks ran on Node.js v18.17.1
integration.platforms: any WebAssembly host (browsers, Node.js, Deno, Bun); Cloudflare Workers (issue #54) and Expo/React Native (issue #57) are open requests; a Bun 1.2.11 CompileError at byte 150 (issue #98, maintainer suspected SIMD) was closed without a confirmed cause
integration.thread_safety: Not thread-safe within one instance: one module-global heap, compressor, decompressor and shared key/IV/output buffers; use one instance per worker.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — replaces pako/node:zlib zlib-deflate and gunzip and @cryptography/aes IGE/CTR for MTProto use, but through a different synchronous Uint8Array API with no streaming, levels, gzip compression or CRC check

gotchas: Benchmark-to-shipped gap: mtcute/benchmarks times blobs from vendor/wasm/lib/Makefile (clang -O3 -flto=full; the no-unroll rows add -fno-inline -fno-unroll-loops) built without -msimd128, so neither the shipped mtcute.wasm (different source set) nor the mtcute-simd.wasm that SIMD-capable engines load was measured. The flags are stated in that Makefile and build.sh, correcting the record's 'not stated'; the clang version is not.

gunzip does not verify CRC32: the check sits under #ifdef CRC32, which no Makefile defines, and neither the benchmarked nor the shipped blobs contain a CRC32 table or polynomial, while zlib.gunzipSync and pako.inflate verify the gzip CRC32 inside their timed calls. The gunzip ratios therefore include work the wasm side skips (small against native zlib, larger against pure-JS pako).

Input-trusting wrappers (found by reading src/index.ts and lib/utils/allocator.c, not executed): gunzip sizes its output from the gzip ISIZE trailer (returned as int32) through a bump allocator that ignores memory.grow failure and does not guard 32-bit overflow, so a lying trailer can grow wasm memory permanently or leave the heap pointer past the end; its error paths throw before freeing the input and output blocks; ige256Encrypt/Decrypt write whole 16-byte blocks without checking the length, overrunning the output block when it is not a multiple of 16. MTProto's padded, msg_key-authenticated payloads avoid these.

Packaging drift: the README's '47 KB raw, 24 KB gzipped' is stale (committed mtcute.wasm 57,363 B, 25,982 B with gzip -9; SIMD blob 59,241 B), and the Dockerfile runs plain make, whose default goal builds only mtcute.wasm, then copies mtcute-simd.wasm.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick hash-wasm when you only need hashes (wider algorithm set, streaming API), and fast-pako or zip.js's wasm zlib for general-purpose gzip/zlib with streaming and CRC checks; pick @mtcute/wasm when you need the MTProto set (AES-IGE/CTR, zlib deflate, gunzip, SHA-1/256) synchronously in one blob of about 26 KB gzipped.
verified_claims_summary: Author-run mtcute/benchmarks (AMD Ryzen 7 5700U, Node.js v18.17.1, NixOS; 2 s warm-up then ten 1 s samples per child process) shows libdeflate-wasm gunzip at 4,981 vs 1,409 ops/s for pako (3.5x) and 3,301 for Node zlib (1.5x) on 73 KB randomised JSON, tgcrypto-wasm AES-IGE at 135 vs 58 MB/s for @cryptography/aes (2.3x) and teeny-sha1 at 281 vs 138 MB/s for rusha, all on standalone non-SIMD blobs rather than the shipped package. Native OpenSSL or the tgcrypto Node addon beats the wasm crypto by 1.7x to 13x at 73 KB.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-10-07, @mtcute/wasm 0.32.0 on npm) and copyable (MIT with LGPL-3.0 AES sources), but the benchmark repo dates from 2023 and times unshipped non-SIMD blobs, part of the gunzip win comes from skipping CRC32, and the input-trusting gunzip and IGE wrappers need validation before reuse outside MTProto.
